title: Leprosy (Hansen Disease)
subject: Medicine
summary: Leprosy is a chronic infection by Mycobacterium leprae causing skin lesions and peripheral nerve loss. Diagnosis relies on clinical pattern and simple skin smears; treatment is multidrug therapy with rifampicin, dapsone and clofazimine.

sections.p: Leprosy is a granulomatous infection of skin and peripheral nerves caused by Mycobacterium leprae. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by slit‑skin smear microscopy or, where available, PCR.
b: Typical hypopigmented or erythematous macules with loss of sensation
Thickened peripheral nerves palpable in the ulnar, common peroneal or posterior tibial distribution
Positive acid‑fast bacilli on slit‑skin smear (≥1 bacillus per 100 fields) confirms the disease

sections.p: The Ridley‑Jopling classification grades disease from tuberculoid (paucibacillary) to lepromatous (multibacillary) based on lesion count, smear grade and immune response.
b: Paucibacillary: ≤5 skin lesions, negative or scant smear (0‑1+)
Multibacillary: >5 lesions or smear ≥2+
WHO operational classification uses the same cut‑offs for treatment decisions

sections.p: Leprosy is transmitted mainly by prolonged close contact with untreated patients; the organism thrives in cool skin areas.
b: Mycobacterium leprae infection – endemic in East Africa, especially rural and tribal communities
Co‑infection with HIV may increase risk of atypical presentations
Living in overcrowded households with poor ventilation

sections.p: Patients present with a combination of skin and nerve findings that evolve over months to years.
b: Hypopigmented, anesthetic macules or plaques; may be raised or nodular in lepromatous form
Peripheral nerve thickening with loss of sensation, especially in hands and feet
Loss of eyebrows (madarosis) and nasal collapse in advanced disease
Secondary ulceration or secondary infection of anesthetic areas

sections.p: In low‑resource settings, simple tests guide diagnosis and classification.

t.b: Confirms presence of bacilli and determines paucibacillary vs multibacillary; if unavailable, rely on lesion count and nerve exam
Provides definitive diagnosis and classification when smear is negative; not essential if clinical picture is classic
Detects loss of protective sensation; helps map nerve involvement and monitor treatment response

t.a: Basic blood count and liver function
t.b: Baseline for monitoring drug toxicity; if labs unavailable, monitor clinically for skin rash, jaundice, or neuropathy

sections.p: Untreated disease can lead to irreversible disability and systemic involvement.
b: Rapid progression of nerve loss causing foot drop or claw hand
Severe ulceration with secondary bacterial infection
Erythema nodosum leprosum (immune complex reaction) causing fever and painful nodules
Eye involvement leading to corneal ulceration and blindness

sections.p: Standard WHO multidrug therapy (MDT) is given for 6‑12 months depending on classification; steroids are added for severe nerve inflammation.
b: Rifampicin (bactericidal) – core drug, given monthly supervised dose
Dapsone (bacteriostatic) – daily dose, avoids resistance when combined with rifampicin
Clofazimine (anti‑inflammatory) – added in multibacillary disease; causes skin discoloration but is well tolerated
Prednisone for acute neuritis or erythema nodosum leprosum – short course to reduce inflammation
Avoid monotherapy to prevent resistance; avoid fluoroquinolones unless indicated for co‑infection

sections.p: Regular monitoring of lesions, nerve function and drug side effects is essential; contact tracing reduces transmission.
b: Monthly clinical review during MDT; assess lesion size, smear status if available, and sensory testing
Educate patients on foot care, protective footwear and wound hygiene
Screen household contacts; give single‑dose rifampicin prophylaxis to eligible contacts
Vaccination with BCG may confer partial protection in endemic areas

sections.p: Several dermatologic and neuropathic conditions mimic leprosy.
b: Cutaneous tuberculosis – similar granulomas but usually ulcerative and not associated with peripheral neuropathy
Sarcoidosis – non‑caseating granulomas, lacks loss of sensation and nerve thickening
Fungal infections (e.g., chromoblastomycosis) – verrucous lesions, no nerve involvement
Diabetic peripheral neuropathy – symmetric stocking‑glove loss, no skin lesions

sections.p: Certain tests may be falsely negative or give a misleading picture.
b: Slit‑skin smear can be negative in early tuberculoid disease; clinical judgment is crucial
Skin biopsy may miss bacilli in paucibacillary cases; do not rule out disease solely on histology
Peripheral nerve thickening can be subtle; use palpation of multiple sites

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden loss of motor function in a limb
Severe foot ulcer with spreading cellulitis
Acute eye pain or vision loss

faq.q: Why does leprosy cause loss of sensation before visible skin change?
faq.a: M. leprae invades Schwann cells, causing segmental demyelination and nerve dysfunction before the skin lesions become obvious.
Yes, WHO‑recommended MDT cures >95 % of patients when completed.
Transmission requires prolonged close contact; casual contact rarely spreads the disease.

exam: A patient presents with a single hypopigmented, anesthetic patch on the forearm and a thickened ulnar nerve – what is your next diagnostic step and why? — Perform a slit‑skin smear to classify paucibacillary vs multibacillary disease; if unavailable, count lesions and assess nerve involvement.
How does the Ridley‑Jopling classification influence treatment duration? — Paucibacillary (≤5 lesions) receives 6 months MDT; multibacillary (>5 lesions or positive smear) receives 12 months MDT.

A lepromatous patient develops painful nodules and fever – what complication is this and how do you manage it? — Erythema nodosum leprosum; treat with high‑dose prednisone or thalidomide if available.
Why is rifampicin given under supervision each month rather than daily? — To ensure adherence, prevent resistance, and exploit its strong bactericidal effect on M. leprae.

A patient on MDT develops a rash and jaundice – which drug is most likely responsible and what is your action? — Dapsone can cause hypersensitivity hepatitis; stop dapsone and continue rifampicin and clofazimine with close monitoring.

What foot care advice would you give to a patient with sensory loss due to leprosy? — Daily inspection, use of protective footwear, keep feet clean and dry, treat any minor trauma promptly to avoid ulceration.

How would you differentiate tuberculoid leprosy from cutaneous tuberculosis on exam? — Tuberculoid leprosy shows isolated anesthetic patches with nerve thickening; cutaneous TB shows ulcerative or verrucous lesions without sensory loss.

A household contact of a newly diagnosed leprosy case asks about prophylaxis – what is recommended? — Single‑dose rifampicin (SDR) for eligible contacts, combined with education on early symptom detection.
